claim: Changes in chromosome number impair fitness by disrupting the balance of gene expression.
source: Changes in chromosome number impair fitness by disrupting the balance of gene expression.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about aneuploidy effects.

claim: Expression of all X-linked transgenes is balanced between XX hermaphrodites and XO males.
source: Using single-copy transgenes integrated throughout the Caenorhabditis elegans genome, we show that expression of all X-linked transgenes is balanced between XX hermaphrodites and XO males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgene expression studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proximity of a dosage compensation complex (DCC) binding site (rex site) is not necessary to repress X-linked transgenes.
source: However, proximity of a dosage compensation complex (DCC) binding site (rex site) is neither necessary to repress X-linked transgenes nor sufficient to repress transgenes on autosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing transgene repression independent of rex site proximity.

claim: Proximity of a DCC binding site (rex site) is not sufficient to repress transgenes on autosomes.
source: However, proximity of a dosage compensation complex (DCC) binding site (rex site) is neither necessary to repress X-linked transgenes nor sufficient to repress transgenes on autosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing autosomal transgenes are not repressed even with nearby rex sites.

claim: X is broadly permissive for dosage compensation.
source: Thus, X is broadly permissive for dosage compensation, and the DCC acts via a chromosome-wide mechanism to balance transcription between sexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing all X-linked transgenes undergo dosage compensation regardless of position.

claim: The DCC acts via a chromosome-wide mechanism to balance transcription between sexes.
source: Thus, X is broadly permissive for dosage compensation, and the DCC acts via a chromosome-wide mechanism to balance transcription between sexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all X-linked transgenes are dosage compensated regardless of proximity to DCC binding sites.

claim: No analogous X-chromosome-wide mechanism balances transcription between X and autosomes.
source: In contrast, no analogous X-chromosome-wide mechanism balances transcription between X and autosomes: expression of compensated hermaphrodite X-linked transgenes is half that of autosomal transgenes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing expression levels of X-linked and autosomal transgenes.

claim: Expression of compensated hermaphrodite X-linked transgenes is half that of autosomal transgenes.
source: In contrast, no analogous X-chromosome-wide mechanism balances transcription between X and autosomes: expression of compensated hermaphrodite X-linked transgenes is half that of autosomal transgenes.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative expression data from transgene experiments.

claim: The results argue against an X-chromosome dosage compensation model contingent upon rex-directed positioning of X relative to the nuclear periphery.
source: Furthermore, our results argue against an X-chromosome dosage compensation model contingent upon rex-directed positioning of X relative to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH experiments and transgene expression data that contradict predictions of the nuclear positioning model.

claim: Aneuploidy occurs in most solid tumors.
source: Aneuploidy occurs in most solid tumors and is a major cause of severe developmental defects and spontaneous abortions (Siegel and Amon, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Aneuploidy is a major cause of severe developmental defects and spontaneous abortions.
source: Aneuploidy occurs in most solid tumors and is a major cause of severe developmental defects and spontaneous abortions (Siegel and Amon, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The disparity in X-chromosome dose between 1X males and 2X females caused by sex-determination mechanisms has evolved to be well tolerated.
source: Unlike pathological imbalances in chromosome dose, the disparity in X-chromosome dose between 1X males and 2X females caused by sex-determination mechanisms has evolved to be well tolerated (Charlesworth, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: For humans, the X and Y sex chromosomes both originated from a single pair of homologous autosomes.
source: For humans, although the X and Y sex chromosomes are genetically distinct, both originated from a single pair of homologous autosomes (Charlesworth, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on sex chromosome evolution.

claim: The differentiation of an autosome pair into two different sex chromosomes was proposed to begin when one homolog acquired a male-determining gene.
source: The differentiation of an autosome pair into two different sex chromosomes was proposed to begin when one homolog acquired a male-determining gene, thereby converting the homologs into a proto-Y and a proto-X (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2000; Bachtrog, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on sex chromosome evolution models.

claim: As recombination ceased between the proto-Y and proto-X, the proto-Y could accumulate other male beneficial alleles but would degenerate into a gene-poor Y chromosome.
source: As recombination ceased between the proto-Y and proto-X, the proto-Y could accumulate other male beneficial alleles, but the recombination isolation would cause it to degenerate into a gene-poor Y chromosome that did little more than specify male sexual fate.
evidence: This claim is based on established models of sex chromosome evolution cited in the manuscript.

claim: In C. elegans, sex chromosomes likely arose from a pair of ancestral autosomes through a similar mechanism to mammals, but with Y-chromosome degradation progressing until the Y was lost completely.
source: In the nematode C. elegans, sex chromosomes also likely arose from a pair of ancestral autosomes through a similar mechanism, but with Y-chromosome degradation progressing until the Y was lost completely (Charlesworth, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on nematode sex chromosome evolution.

claim: The demise of Y as a male-determining chromosome in C. elegans was enabled by the emergence of a sex-determination mechanism that utilized the ratio of X chromosomes to sets of autosomes.
source: The demise of Y as a male-determining chromosome was enabled by the emergence of a different sex-determination mechanism, one that utilized the ratio of X chromosomes to sets of autosomes (ploidy) to specify male (1X:2A) vs. hermaphrodite (2X:2A) sexual fates (Nigon, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on C. elegans sex determination.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster increases X-linked gene expression two-fold in males to balance gene expression with that in females.
source: For the XX/XY species Drosophila melanogaster, potential complications caused by males having one X chromosome were averted by the co-evolution of a dosage compensation mechanism that operates by doubling gene expression from the single male X chromosome. Elevating X expression in males balanced gene expression with that from the two female X chromosomes, while maintaining similar expression between the single X and the two ancestral autosomes (Figure 1B) (Lucchesi and Kuroda, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on Drosophila dosage compensation.

claim: Placental mammals and C. elegans developed mechanisms of dosage compensation that equalized X-chromosome expression between the sexes by reducing X-linked gene expression by half in XX animals.
source: In contrast, other animals including placental mammals and the nematode C. elegans developed mechanisms of dosage compensation that equalized X-chromosome expression between the sexes by reducing X-linked gene expression by half in XX animals (Figure 1C) (Meyer, 2010; Galupa and Heard, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mammalian and nematode dosage compensation.

claim: Susumo Ohno proposed that loss of genes from the degenerating Y chromosome was compensated via two sequential evolutionary steps for mammals.
source: For mammals, Susumo Ohno proposed that loss of genes from the degenerating Y chromosome was compensated via two sequential evolutionary steps (Figure 1D) (Ohno, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ohno's original hypothesis.

claim: Comparison between the extant mammalian X chromosome and the orthologous chicken autosome failed to reveal evidence for X-chromosome-wide upregulation in placental mammals.
source: Comparison between the extant mammalian X chromosome and the orthologous chicken autosome failed to reveal evidence for X-chromosome-wide upregulation in placental mammals (Julien et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature testing Ohno's hypothesis in mammals.

claim: In placental mammals, genes on the single active X chromosome in males and females are expressed, on average, at half the level of the orthologous pair of autosomes.
source: In these species, genes on the single active X chromosome in males and females are expressed, on average, at half the level of the orthologous pair of autosomes, contrary to Ohno's hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is based on prior literature cited in the manuscript that tested Ohno's hypothesis.

claim: Evidence in favor of Ohno's hypothesis exists in marsupials.
source: In contrast, evidence in favor of Ohno's hypothesis exists in marsupials, suggesting that X-chromosome upregulation may have accompanied sex-chromosome evolution in some lineages but not others (Julien et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on marsupial dosage compensation.

claim: The average overall expression of all genes on extant autosomes was assumed to serve as a proxy for expression of the proto-X chromosome in some C. elegans studies.
source: In the absence of information about orthology, the assumption was made in some studies that the average overall expression of all genes on extant autosomes would serve as a proxy for expression of the proto-X chromosome (Deng et al., 2011; Kruesi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies that made this assumption.

claim: Average gene expression varies widely (1.9 fold) among the five different autosomes in C. elegans.
source: However, this assumption is undermined by the unexpected observation we report here that average gene expression varies widely (1.9 fold) among the five different autosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and GRO-seq data presented in the manuscript figures.

claim: X-chromosome gene expression undergoes transcriptional silencing in germ cells of XX and XO animals.
source: Second, X-chromosome gene expression undergoes transcriptional silencing in germ cells of XX and XO animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) (Reinke et al., 2000; Kelly et al., 2002; Deng et al., 2011; Gaydos et al., 2012), which comprise 68% of all adult cells (Crittenden et al., 2006; Morgan et al., 2010), causing tests of Ohno's hypothesis that quantify adult gene expression (Xiong et al., 2010) to underestimate X expression by about 50%.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and data presented in the manuscript figures.

claim: Germ cells comprise 68% of all adult cells in C. elegans.
source: Second, X-chromosome gene expression undergoes transcriptional silencing in germ cells of XX and XO animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) (Reinke et al., 2000; Kelly et al., 2002; Deng et al., 2011; Gaydos et al., 2012), which comprise 68% of all adult cells (Crittenden et al., 2006; Morgan et al., 2010), causing tests of Ohno's hypothesis that quantify adult gene expression (Xiong et al., 2010) to underestimate X expression by about 50%.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Not all genes on X are dosage compensated in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, as in mammals, not all genes on X are dosage compensated (Carrel and Willard, 2005; Jans et al., 2009; Kruesi et al., 2013), and the factors that determine whether a gene becomes dosage compensated or escapes from dosage compensation are not known.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dosage compensation complex (DCC) in C. elegans is homologous to condensin.
source: Balancing X-chromosome gene expression between the sexes is achieved in C. elegans by a dosage compensation complex (DCC) that is homologous to condensin (Csankovszki et al., 2009; Mets and Meyer, 2009; Meyer, 2010), a conserved protein complex that controls the compaction and resolution of all mitotic and meiotic chromosomes prior to their segregation (Wood et al., 2010; Hirano, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The DCC is recruited to both X chromosomes of hermaphrodites by cis-acting regulatory elements distributed throughout X called recruitment elements on X (rex sites).
source: The DCC is recruited to both X chromosomes of hermaphrodites by cis-acting regulatory elements distributed throughout X called recruitment elements on X (rex sites).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about DCC recruitment cited in the manuscript.

claim: Rex sites include DNA motifs that are highly enriched on X chromosomes and important for DCC binding.
source: These sites include DNA motifs that are highly enriched on X chromosomes and important for DCC binding (Csankovszki et al., 2004; McDonel et al., 2006; Ercan et al., 2007; Jans et al., 2009; Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The DCC remodels the topology of X while reducing the expression from both hermaphrodite X chromosomes by half.
source: Once bound to X, the DCC remodels the topology of X, while reducing the expression from both hermaphrodite X chromosomes by half to balance gene expression between the sexes (Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All transgenes integrated onto C. elegans X chromosomes are dosage compensated, regardless of their position on X and proximity to an endogenous rex site.
source: We first show here that all transgenes integrated onto C. elegans X chromosomes are dosage compensated, regardless of their position on X and hence their proximity to an endogenous rex site.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgene expression studies.

claim: Integration of transgenes onto autosomes, either with or without an adjacent DCC-bound rex site, failed to elicit DCC-mediated repression in hermaphrodites.
source: Furthermore, integration of the same transgenes onto autosomes, either with or without an adjacent DCC-bound rex site, failed to elicit DCC-mediated repression in hermaphrodites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgene expression studies.

claim: DCC binding to a nearby rex site is not sufficient to trigger dosage compensation of a gene.
source: Thus, DCC binding to a nearby rex site is not sufficient to trigger dosage compensation of a gene, nor is it necessary.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing autosomal transgenes with nearby rex sites are not dosage compensated.

claim: DCC binding to a nearby rex site is not necessary to trigger dosage compensation of a gene.
source: Thus, DCC binding to a nearby rex site is not sufficient to trigger dosage compensation of a gene, nor is it necessary.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing X-linked transgenes without nearby rex sites are dosage compensated.

claim: In dosage-compensated XX animals, the per-copy expression of X-linked transgenes is half that of autosomal transgenes.
source: We show that in dosage-compensated (i.e. down regulated) XX animals, the per-copy expression of X-linked transgenes is half, not equivalent to, the per-copy expression of their counterparts on autosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing transgene expression levels.

claim: The per-copy expression of hemizygous X-linked transgenes in XO animals is equivalent to the per-copy expression of their autosomal counterparts.
source: In addition, the per-copy expression of hemizygous X-linked transgenes in XO animals is equivalent to, not double, the per-copy expression of their autosomal counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing transgene expression levels in males.

claim: Both findings (X-linked transgene expression in XX and XO animals) are inconsistent with a chromosome-wide mechanism of upregulation.
source: Both findings are inconsistent with a chromosome-wide mechanism of upregulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: If upregulation did occur to compensate for gradual loss of genes during X-chromosome evolution, it proceeded by the emergence of diverse gene-specific mechanisms.
source: Our results suggest that if upregulation did occur to compensate for gradual loss of genes during X-chromosome evolution, it proceeded by the emergence of diverse gene-specific mechanisms that would compensate for their reduced dose.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: A recent model proposes that rex sites target X chromosomes to the nuclear periphery in males to increase gene expression.
source: Finally, our analysis of X-chromosome regulation, combined with chromosome localization studies, allowed us to evaluate a recent, speculative model of X-chromosome dosage compensation, which proposes that rex sites target X chromosomes to the nuclear periphery in males to increase gene expression, while DCC binding to rex sites in hermaphrodites relocates X to the interior, thereby reducing gene expression to achieve dosage compensation (Sharma et al., 2014; Sharma and Meister, 2015).
evidence: This claim describes a model from prior literature.

claim: Results provide strong evidence against the nuclear positioning model of dosage compensation proposed by Sharma et al.
source: Results presented here provide strong evidence against this model of dosage compensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgene expression and FISH studies.

claim: All 28 X-linked reporters were repressed by the DCC.
source: Quantification of reporter mRNA levels to assess whether transgenes integrated across X were dosage compensated revealed that all 28 X-linked reporters were repressed by the DCC.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All X-linked reporters had increased expression in sdc-2(RNAi) versus control L1s, regardless of their location on X and the origin of their promoter.
source: All had increased expression in sdc-2(RNAi) versus control L1s, regardless of their location on X and the origin of their promoter, whether from the C. elegans X chromosome (eft-4), C. elegans autosomes (eft-3 and dpy-30), or a C. briggsae autosome (Cbr-unc-119) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The extent of DCC-mediated repression ranged from 1.3 to 3.7-fold for X-linked transgenes.
source: The extent of DCC-mediated repression ranged from 1.3 to 3.7-fold, consistent with the range observed for endogenous dosage-compensated X-linked genes assessed by RNA-seq (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and comparison with RNA-seq data.

claim: The X-linked reporters had equivalent expression in XX and XO animals at the L1/L2 stage.
source: We also found that the X-linked reporters had equivalent expression in XX and XO animals at the L1/L2 stage. That is, the total level of transgene expression from the two X chromosomes of hermaphrodites was not statistically different from the total level of transgene expression from the single X of males (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of 36 transgenes on autosomes was not increased by disrupting dosage compensation.
source: In contrast to transgenes on X, expression of 36 transgenes on autosomes was not increased by disrupting dosage compensation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: DCC binding near an endogenous X-linked gene was neither necessary nor sufficient for the dosage compensation of the gene in prior genome-wide studies.
source: Prior genome-wide studies found that DCC binding near an endogenous X-linked gene was neither necessary nor sufficient for the dosage compensation of the gene (Jans et al., 2009; Kruesi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Binding of both DPY-27 and SDC-3 to the transgenes was negligible compared to DCC binding at the strong rex sites rex-1 and rex-32.
source: Binding of both DPY-27 and SDC-3 to the transgenes was negligible compared to DCC binding at the strong rex sites rex-1 and rex-32 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Transgenes lacking DCC binding are nonetheless repressed by the DCC, indicating that local DCC binding is not required for dosage compensation.
source: The finding that transgenes lacking DCC binding are nonetheless repressed by the DCC indicates that local DCC binding is not required for dosage compensation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ChIP and expression data.

claim: For transgenes on X, the increase in expression in sdc-2(RNAi) animals was not correlated with their proximity to a rex site.
source: We found that for transgenes on X, the increase in expression in sdc-2(RNAi) animals was not correlated with their proximity to a rex site.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transgene expression data relative to rex site positions.

claim: A nearby rex site is not essential for the compensation of a gene.
source: Thus, a nearby rex site is not essential for the compensation of a gene.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between rex site proximity and dosage compensation.

claim: DCC binding to a nearby dox site is not essential for the compensation of a gene.
source: Furthermore, DCC binding to a nearby dox site is also not essential for the compensation of a gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transgene expression data relative to dox site positions.

claim: The DCC can act at a distance to control expression of foreign genes integrated across the X chromosome.
source: Together, these data indicate that the DCC can act at a distance to control expression of foreign genes integrated across the X chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing dosage compensation independent of local DCC binding.

claim: SDC-3 binding at the ectopic rex-32 sites on autosomes was similar to, or greater than, binding at the endogenous rex-32 site on X.
source: SDC-3 binding at the ectopic rex-32 sites on autosomes was similar to, or greater than, binding at the endogenous rex-32 site on X (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: DPY-27 occupancy at the ectopic rex-32 site on chromosome I was equivalent to DPY-27 occupancy at the rex-32 site on X.
source: Similarly, DPY-27 occupancy at the ectopic rex-32 site on chromosome I was equivalent to DPY-27 occupancy at the rex-32 site on X (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of seven of eight reporters was not significantly reduced compared to expression of the same reporters integrated at the same autosomal sites without a rex site, despite strong DCC binding to rex sites closely linked to the autosomal reporters.
source: Despite strong DCC binding to rex sites closely linked to the autosomal reporters, expression of seven of eight reporters was not significantly reduced compared to expression of the same reporters integrated at the same autosomal sites without a rex site (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: In sdc-2(RNAi) XX animals with very low levels DCC binding, expression of six of eight autosomal reporters with closely linked rex sites was not elevated compared to expression of the same rex-linked autosomal reporters in control XX animals with high levels of DCC binding.
source: Furthermore, in sdc-2(RNAi) XX animals with very low levels DCC binding, expression of six of eight autosomal reporters with closely linked rex sites was not elevated compared to expression of the same rex-linked autosomal reporters in control XX animals with high levels of DCC binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing expression in control and sdc-2(RNAi) animals.

claim: Strong DCC binding adjacent to a gene is generally not sufficient to regulate its expression.
source: These results indicate that strong DCC binding adjacent to a gene is generally not sufficient to regulate its expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on autosomal transgenes with adjacent rex sites.

claim: Results strongly support a model in which DCC binding causes global changes to the X chromosome, likely by remodeling X topology to elicit chromosome-wide gene repression.
source: Our results strongly support a model in which DCC binding causes global changes to the X chromosome, likely by remodeling X topology (Crane et al., 2015) to elicit chromosome-wide gene repression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to prior work on X topology.

claim: The average total expression of all X-linked transgenes in XX animals (2 copies) was 56% of the average total expression of all transgenes on autosomes (2 copies).
source: We found that the average total expression of all X-linked transgenes in XX animals (2 copies) was 56% of the average total expression of all transgenes on autosomes (2 copies) (p<0.0001, 95% CI of the mean between 0.497 and 0.620) (Figure 6A, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The relative level of transgene expression on X compared to autosomes differs significantly from the ratio of 1 predicted by an Ohno-like model of X chromosome-wide upregulation.
source: Thus, the relative level of transgene expression on X compared to autosomes differs significantly from the ratio of 1 predicted by an Ohno-like model of X chromosome-wide upregulation (One Sample t-test, p<0.001) and is not significantly different from the ratio of 0.5 predicted by the lack of a general upregulation mechanism (One Sample t-test, p=0.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of transgene expression data.

claim: The relative level of transgene expression on X compared to autosomes is not significantly different from the ratio of 0.5 predicted by the lack of a general upregulation mechanism.
source: Thus, the relative level of transgene expression on X compared to autosomes differs significantly from the ratio of 1 predicted by an Ohno-like model of X chromosome-wide upregulation (One Sample t-test, p<0.001) and is not significantly different from the ratio of 0.5 predicted by the lack of a general upregulation mechanism (One Sample t-test, p=0.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of transgene expression data.

claim: Depending on the reporter, X chromosome transgenes were expressed on average between 44% and 68% of their autosomal counterparts.
source: Depending on the reporter, X chromosome transgenes were expressed on average between 44% and 68% of their autosomal counterparts (Figure 6B), again arguing against a chromosome-wide mechanism to increase gene expression on X chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of a single transgene on the male X was not different from expression of a single transgene on one of the autosomal homologs.
source: We found to the contrary that expression of a single transgene on the male X was not different from expression of a single transgene on one of the autosomal homologs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Reporters had only minimal variability in expression when integrated at different sites along the X chromosome or autosomes.
source: We were able to reach the robust conclusion that expression of transgenes on X is significantly lower than expression of transgenes on autosomes because our reporters had only minimal variability in expression when integrated at different sites along the X chromosome or autosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transgene expression variability presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nuclear positioning model predicts that in males the transgenes on X should have elevated expression relative to transgenes on autosomes due to a rex-dependent association of X with the nuclear periphery.
source: First, the nuclear positioning model predicts that in males the transgenes on X should have elevated expression relative to transgenes on autosomes due to a rex-dependent association of X with the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the nuclear positioning model proposed by Sharma et al.

claim: In males, expression of single-copy transgenes on the sole X chromosome was not different from expression of single-copy transgenes inserted on only one of two homologous autosomes, contrary to the nuclear positioning model.
source: However, we found that in males, expression of single-copy transgenes on the sole X chromosome was not different from expression of single-copy transgenes inserted on only one of two homologous autosomes (Figure 6C), contrary to the nuclear positioning model of dosage compensation (Sharma et al., 2014; Sharma and Meister, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Depletion of the DCC did not significantly increase the expression of any of the 12 rex-linked reporter transgenes on X chromosomes or autosomes compared to their expression at the same locations without a rex site.
source: We found that in XX animals, depletion of the DCC did not significantly increase the expression of any of the 12 rex-linked reporter transgenes on X chromosomes or autosomes compared to their expression at the same locations without a rex site (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of DCC binding in XX animals did not significantly elevate expression for six of eight autosomal reporters with an adjacent rex site.
source: Furthermore, loss of DCC binding in XX animals did not significantly elevate expression for six of eight autosomal reporters with an adjacent rex site (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: DCC binding adjacent to a gene is not sufficient to induce repression of the gene.
source: Thus, DCC binding adjacent to a gene is not sufficient to induce repression of the gene, unlike the expectation from the nuclear positioning model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on autosomal transgenes with adjacent rex sites.

claim: Rex sites in autosomes, validated for DCC binding in wild-type XX animals, did not preferentially recruit flanking autosomal DNA to the nuclear periphery under conditions in which DCC binding was prohibited.
source: Third, using the same approach as (Sharma et al., 2014) but contrary to their single result, we found that rex sites in autosomes, validated for DCC binding in wild-type XX animals, did not preferentially recruit flanking autosomal DNA to the nuclear periphery under conditions in which DCC binding was prohibited (Figure 7 A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The autosomal regions of chromosome I and IV that flank the integrated ectopic rex-32 site did not localize more frequently to the nuclear periphery in either younger or older XO embryos compared to age-matched XX embryos.
source: Specifically, the autosomal regions of chromosome I and IV that flank the integrated ectopic rex-32 site did not localize more frequently to the nuclear periphery (zone 1 vs. zones 2 and 3) in either younger (50–140 cells) or older (>200 cells) XO embryos (both lacking DCC binding at rex-32) compared to age-matched XX embryos (both proficient in DCC binding at rex-32) (Figure 7 A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Autosomal loci adjacent to a rex insertion were not localized more frequently to the nuclear periphery in younger or older XO embryos than the same autosomal loci in age-matched XO embryos lacking the rex insertion.
source: In addition, autosomal loci adjacent to a rex insertion were not localized more frequently to the nuclear periphery in younger or older XO embryos than the same autosomal loci in age-matched XO embryos lacking the rex insertion. For comparisons involving younger embryos, p>0.5; for those involving older embryos, p>0.1 (chi-square tests).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data and statistical analysis.

claim: An ectopic rex site lacking DCC binding is insufficient to relocate flanking autosomal DNA to the nuclear periphery.
source: Thus, an ectopic rex site lacking DCC binding is insufficient to relocate flanking autosomal DNA to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the FISH data on autosomal rex sites.

claim: All five endogenous rex sites tested on X were not preferentially recruited to the nuclear periphery in XO embryos in either the 50-140-cell stage or the > 200-cell stage compared to age-matched XX embryos.
source: Fourth, all five endogenous rex sites tested on X, including three in the center (rex-33, rex-47 and rex-8) and two toward one end (rex-32 and rex-23), were not preferentially recruited to the nuclear periphery in XO embryos in either the 50-140-cell stage or the > 200-cell stage compared to age-matched XX embryos (p>0.1, chi-square test) (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data presented in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: For rex-23, older XX embryos showed more peripheral localization than older XO embryos, but both sexes showed less peripheral localization than expected by random chance.
source: Indeed, for rex-23 the opposite was found: older XX embryos showed more peripheral localization than older XO embryos (p<0.001, chi-square test), but both sexes showed less peripheral localization than expected by random chance (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data and statistical analysis.

claim: For rex-47, younger embryos of both sexes had enrichment in the peripheral-most zone, but peripheral enrichment in XO embryos was not greater than in XX.
source: For rex-47, younger embryos of both sexes had enrichment in the peripheral-most zone (p=0.008), but peripheral enrichment in XO embryos was not greater than in XX.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data and statistical analysis.

claim: The dosage compensation process acts on a chromosome-wide basis to reduce expression of all X-linked transgenes in XX animals, regardless of their source of promoter, position on X, or proximity to a dosage compensation complex (DCC) binding site.
source: Our analysis showed that the dosage compensation process, which equalizes X expression between the sexes by reducing expression of endogenous X-linked genes in hermaphrodites, acts on a chromosome-wide basis to reduce expression of all X-linked transgenes in XX animals, regardless of their source of promoter, position on X, or proximity to a dosage compensation complex (DCC) binding site.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: Close proximity to a DCC binding site is unnecessary to reduce X-linked transgene expression.
source: Not only is close proximity to a DCC binding site unnecessary to reduce X-linked transgene expression, it is also insufficient to repress expression of autosomal transgenes co-integrated with a DCC binding site.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: Close proximity to a DCC binding site is insufficient to repress expression of autosomal transgenes co-integrated with a DCC binding site.
source: Not only is close proximity to a DCC binding site unnecessary to reduce X-linked transgene expression, it is also insufficient to repress expression of autosomal transgenes co-integrated with a DCC binding site.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: The cis-acting DCC regulatory sites act cumulatively to create an environment on X that is broadly permissive for repression of endogenous and engineered genes.
source: This finding reinforces the model that the cis-acting DCC regulatory sites act cumulatively to create an environment on X that is broadly permissive for repression of endogenous and engineered genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: Transgenes on hermaphrodite X chromosomes were expressed at half the level of their autosomal counterparts, contrary to a chromosome-wide mechanism to balance gene expression across the genome.
source: We found that transgenes on hermaphrodite X chromosomes were expressed at half the level of their autosomal counterparts, contrary to a chromosome-wide mechanism to balance gene expression across the genome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: Prior genome-wide studies supported a chromosome-wide mechanism by demonstrating no correlation between DCC binding in or near an endogenous gene and the dosage compensation status of the gene.
source: Prior genome-wide studies supported a chromosome-wide mechanism by demonstrating no correlation between DCC binding in or near an endogenous gene and the dosage compensation status of the gene (Jans et al., 2009; Kruesi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dosage compensation of transgenes integrated on X did not require local DCC binding or even close proximity to a strong DCC recruitment site.
source: First, dosage compensation of transgenes integrated on X did not require local DCC binding or even close proximity to a strong DCC recruitment site.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression and ChIP.

claim: Only transgenes on X were responsive to the dosage compensation process.
source: Second, only transgenes on X were responsive to the dosage compensation process.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression.

claim: Close proximity of strong DCC recruitment sites to transgenes on autosomes did not elicit gene repression.
source: Third, close proximity of strong DCC recruitment sites to transgenes on autosomes did not elicit gene repression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on autosomal transgene expression.

claim: In wild-type XX embryos, expression of transgenes on autosomes was not lower in the presence of nearby rex sites than in their absence.
source: That is, in wild-type XX embryos, expression of transgenes on autosomes was not lower in the presence of nearby rex sites than in their absence, and transgenes co-inserted with rex sites were not generally increased in expression in dosage-compensation-defective mutants, further demonstrating that local DCC binding is not sufficient to establish dosage compensation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on autosomal transgene expression.

claim: Transgenes co-inserted with rex sites were not generally increased in expression in dosage-compensation-defective mutants.
source: That is, in wild-type XX embryos, expression of transgenes on autosomes was not lower in the presence of nearby rex sites than in their absence, and transgenes co-inserted with rex sites were not generally increased in expression in dosage-compensation-defective mutants, further demonstrating that local DCC binding is not sufficient to establish dosage compensation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on autosomal transgene expression.

claim: The promoter of an X-linked gene does not dictate the dosage compensation status.
source: The promoter of an X-linked gene also does not dictate the dosage compensation status. Although the eft-4 gene is dosage compensated at its endogenous location on X, and X-linked transgenes driven by the eft-4 promoter are dosage compensated, eft-4-driven transgenes on autosomes are not.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on transgenes with different promoters.

claim: The promoter does not transmit responsiveness to the dosage compensation process.
source: Thus, the promoter does not transmit responsiveness to the dosage compensation process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on transgenes with different promoters.

claim: Rex sites act in concert and over long distance to establish an X-chromosome environment that promotes reduction of gene expression across the entire chromosome.
source: Our data support the model that rex sites act in concert and over long distance to establish an X-chromosome environment that promotes reduction of gene expression across the entire chromosome, even for endogenous and engineered genes that lack DCC binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on transgene expression and DCC binding.

claim: DCC binding at rex sites controls the topology of the entire X chromosome.
source: Our results are in strong agreement with recent studies demonstrating that DCC binding at rex sites controls the topology of the entire X chromosome (Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All engineered transgenes on X were responsive to dosage compensation yet some endogenous X-linked genes escape dosage compensation in C. elegans.
source: All engineered transgenes on X were responsive to dosage compensation yet some endogenous X-linked genes escape dosage compensation in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim combines experimental data from the current study with knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Genes that escape dosage compensation are in close proximity to and interspersed with genes that undergo dosage compensation.
source: These features likely operate locally because genes that escape dosage compensation are in close proximity to and interspersed with genes that undergo dosage compensation (Jans et al., 2009; Kruesi et al., 2013; Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most X-chromosome transgenes in both Drosophila melanogaster and mice are subject to XX/XY dosage compensation.
source: As in C. elegans, most X-chromosome transgenes in both Drosophila melanogaster and mice are subject to XX/XY dosage compensation (Scholnick et al., 1983; Spradling and Rubin, 1983; Krumlauf et al., 1986; Dandolo et al., 1993; Tan et al., 1993; Yang et al., 2012), but in both species, some endogenous genes on X escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In both Drosophila and mice, some endogenous genes on X escape dosage compensation.
source: As in C. elegans, most X-chromosome transgenes in both Drosophila melanogaster and mice are subject to XX/XY dosage compensation (Scholnick et al., 1983; Spradling and Rubin, 1983; Krumlauf et al., 1986; Dandolo et al., 1993; Tan et al., 1993; Yang et al., 2012), but in both species, some endogenous genes on X escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The territory surrounding the mouse gene Kdm5c has two separable regulatory domains that influence X inactivation in opposite ways.
source: In support of an insulation model, the territory surrounding the mouse gene Kdm5c has two separable regulatory domains that influence X inactivation in opposite ways: one causes Kdm5c to escape X inactivation at its endogenous site on X and at ectopic sites on X, and a second region prevents X-linked genes nearby Kdm5c from escaping X inactivation (Horvath et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The discrepancy in conclusions about X-chromosome-wide upregulation between the current study and previous studies results from an incorrect prior assumption that the average expression of all present-day autosomes serves as a reliable proxy for expression of proto-X chromosomes.
source: We propose that the discrepancy in conclusions about X-chromosome-wide upregulation between our current study and previous studies (Deng et al., 2011; Kruesi et al., 2013) results from an incorrect prior assumption that the average expression of all present-day autosomes serves as a reliable proxy for expression of proto-X chromosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing variability in autosomal expression.

claim: The assumption that average expression of all present-day autosomes serves as a proxy for proto-X expression was shown to be incorrect for placental mammals.
source: That assumption was shown to be incorrect for placental mammals (Julien et al., 2012), and our observation that the average expression for each of the five autosomes varies by 1.9-fold undermines that assumption for C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and data from the current study.

claim: A recent C. elegans study compared the expression of 276 genes located on chromosome I in Pristionchus pacificus but on chromosome X in Caenorhabditis due to a chromosome translocation.
source: In a different test of Ohno's hypothesis, a recent C. elegans study compared the expression of 276 genes located on chromosome I in the nematode Pristionchus pacificus but on chromosome X in Caenorhabditis due to a chromosome translocation that occurred after the species' divergence (~ 300 MYA) (Albritton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Albritton et al. study found that in XO animals, the new genes on the C. elegans X chromosome were expressed, on average, at about half the level of their autosomal orthologs in P. pacificus.
source: The study found that in XO animals, the new genes on the C. elegans X chromosome were expressed, on average, at about half the level of their autosomal orthologs in P. pacificus, a result the study concluded is inconsistent with chromosome-wide upregulation of X.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Expression of the 276 genes was higher in somatic cells of C. elegans germlineless XX L4 larvae than in the combination of somatic and germ cells found in fertile, wild-type L4 XX larvae.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we found that expression of the 276 genes was higher in somatic cells of C. elegans germlineless XX L4 larvae than in the combination of somatic and germ cells found in fertile, wild-type L4 XX larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Germline silencing causes an underestimate of somatic gene expression in both sexes.
source: Therefore, germline silencing, which causes an underestimate of somatic gene expression in both sexes (Deng et al., 2011), is a plausible cause for the apparent reduction in expression of genes naturally translocated to X during evolution compared to their expression when sited on autosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In Drosophila, elevation of H4K16Ac is the hallmark of an upregulated male X chromosome.
source: In Drosophila, elevation of H4K16Ac is the hallmark of an upregulated male X chromosome.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila dosage compensation.

claim: H4K16ac was found to be depleted on X chromosomes vs. autosomes of wild-type hermaphrodites and enriched on X vs. autosomes of dosage-compensation-defective hermaphrodites in C. elegans.
source: In the C. elegans studies, H4K16ac was found to be depleted on X chromosomes vs. autosomes of wild-type hermaphrodites and enriched on X vs. autosomes of dosage-compensation-defective hermaphrodites, suggesting an involvement of H4K16Ac in upregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Wells et al., 2012).

claim: Males showed no X-chromosome enrichment of H4K16Ac in C. elegans.
source: However, males showed no X-chromosome enrichment of H4K16Ac, a result that precludes a role for H4K16Ac in X-chromosome upregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Wells et al., 2012).

claim: The lack of global X upregulation in C. elegans is consistent with findings in placental mammals.
source: The lack of global X upregulation in C. elegans is consistent with findings in placental mammals (Julien et al., 2012), suggesting that many organisms tolerated the evolution of sex chromosomes without a global compensation mechanism to correct for reduced X-chromosome gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison with prior literature.

claim: In D. miranda, a fusion between the Y chromosome and an autosome initiated the formation of neo-sex chromosomes about 1 MYA.
source: In D. miranda, a fusion between the Y chromosome and an autosome initiated the formation of these new sex chromosomes about 1 MYA (Bachtrog and Charlesworth, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Since the fusion in D. miranda, almost half of the genes on the neo-Y chromosome were lost or accumulated inactivating mutations.
source: Since the fusion, almost half of the genes on the neo-Y chromosome were lost or accumulated inactivating mutations (Bachtrog et al., 2008; Zhou and Bachtrog, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The neo-X chromosome in D. miranda acquired dosage compensation by upregulating X-chromosome expression in males using the same dosage compensation machinery as in D. melanogaster.
source: The neo-X chromosome acquired dosage compensation by upregulating X-chromosome expression in males using the same dosage compensation machinery as in D. melanogaster (Bone and Kuroda, 1996; Marín et al., 1996; Alekseyenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compensation in D. miranda is far less complete than that for D. melanogaster.
source: However, compensation in D. miranda is far less complete than that for D. melanogaster (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Many genes that were lost from the neo-Y chromosome are not yet upregulated on the D. miranda neo-X chromosome.
source: Many genes that were lost from the neo-Y chromosome are not yet upregulated on the D. miranda neo-X chromosome, suggesting that D. miranda can tolerate hemizygosity of many X-chromosome genes in the male XY sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and inference about tolerance of hemizygosity.

claim: The X is significantly depleted of essential and haploinsufficient genes compared to autosomes in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, gene content on X differs from that on autosomes: the X is significantly depleted of essential and haploinsufficient genes compared to autosomes (Kamath et al., 2003; de Clare et al., 2011; Albritton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A few genes on the C. elegans X chromosome maintain a functional paralog on an autosome.
source: Furthermore, a few genes on the C. elegans X chromosome maintain a functional paralog on an autosome (Maciejowski et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Changes in X-chromosome gene content may have played a role during sex chromosome evolution to accommodate the reduced dose of X-linked genes.
source: Together, these features of X have been proposed to prevent problems caused by germline silencing of X, but changes in X-chromosome gene content may equally well have played a role during sex chromosome evolution to accommodate the reduced dose of X-linked genes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation combining prior literature with the current study's findings.

claim: A balance hypothesis posits that gene dose is especially important for genes that encode subunits of protein complexes.
source: A balance hypothesis, borne out in yeast, posits that gene dose is especially important for genes that encode subunits of protein complexes, because changes in gene dose can disrupt complex formation by altering subunit stoichiometry (Papp et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In aneuploid laboratory yeast strains, post-translational mechanisms, especially protein degradation, were found to attenuate the increase in protein levels caused by the increased dose of specific classes of genes.
source: In recent studies of aneuploid laboratory yeast strains, post-translational mechanisms, especially protein degradation, were found to attenuate the increase in protein levels caused by the increased dose of specific classes of genes, particularly those encoding subunits of multi-protein complexes (Torres et al., 2010; Dephoure et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In wild yeast strains, chromosomal amplifications have been found, but a debate exists over whether an active mode of dosage compensation specifically reduces transcript levels of amplified genes.
source: In wild yeast strains, chromosomal amplifications have been found, but a debate exists over whether an active mode of dosage compensation specifically reduces transcript levels of amplified genes (Hose et al., 2015; Gasch et al., 2016; Torres et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In placental mammals, reduced X-chromosome dose can be compensated in some cases by increasing expression of dose-sensitive genes on X, particularly those producing subunits of large protein complexes.
source: In placental mammals, which lack global X upregulation, reduced X-chromosome dose can be compensated in some cases by increasing expression of dose-sensitive genes on X, particularly those producing subunits of large protein complexes (Pessia et al., 2012), or by decreasing expression of autosomal genes that produce subunits of macromolecular complexes containing proteins encoded by X-linked genes (Julien et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In placental mammals, reduced X-chromosome dose can be compensated by decreasing expression of autosomal genes that produce subunits of macromolecular complexes containing proteins encoded by X-linked genes.
source: In placental mammals, which lack global X upregulation, reduced X-chromosome dose can be compensated in some cases by increasing expression of dose-sensitive genes on X, particularly those producing subunits of large protein complexes (Pessia et al., 2012), or by decreasing expression of autosomal genes that produce subunits of macromolecular complexes containing proteins encoded by X-linked genes (Julien et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mammalian histone methyl transferase complex called MOF acetylates histone H4 on lysine 16 to upregulate expression of a small set of genes on X.
source: While the general mechanisms that govern local changes in mammalian gene expression are not well known, one source of gene regulation is the mammalian histone methyl transferase complex called MOF, which acetylates histone H4 on lysine 16 to upregulate expression of a small set of genes on X (Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: For some X-linked genes, evidence exists for enhanced mRNA stability or enhanced translational efficiency via increased ribosome density as possible mechanisms to compensate for reduced gene dose.
source: In addition, for some X-linked genes, evidence also exists for enhanced mRNA stability or enhanced translational efficiency via increased ribosome density as possible mechanisms to compensate for reduced gene dose (Deng et al., 2013; Faucillion and Larsson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.
